subtitle: 31 · asked her GP about her family history of cancer
opening: Hi. I'm not sure where to start, really.

questions.q: What made you want to come today?
questions.a: My mum had breast cancer when she was 42, and my aunt died of ovarian cancer. I've read that they can run in families, and I want to know whether I should be having screening.

questions.q: How old are you, Megan?
Have you had any health problems yourself, or any breast symptoms?
questions.a: No, I'm well. No lumps or anything.

questions.q: Do you have a partner or any children?
questions.a: No partner at the moment, and no children.

questions.q: Have you ever been pregnant?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: Two younger brothers, Ryan and Luke. They're twins – they're 28.

questions.q: Are Ryan and Luke identical or non-identical twins?
questions.a: Identical. Even Mum mixes them up on the phone.

questions.q: Do you all have the same parents?
questions.a: Ryan, Luke and I do. I've also got a half-brother, Josh. He's 19 – he's Dad's son with his wife, Lisa.
questions.note: This is why the workshop suggests asking ‘Do you all have the same parents?’: half-brothers and half-sisters are easy to miss otherwise.

questions.q: How is your brothers’ health?
questions.a: All three are fine.

questions.q: Are your parents still together?
questions.a: No. They separated when I was ten. Dad married again – Lisa, Josh’s mum.

questions.q: How old is your mum, and how is her health?
questions.a: Mum's 58. She had breast cancer when she was 42. She had an operation and chemotherapy, and she's been well since.

questions.q: And your mum's all clear now, so that's fine?
questions.a: Well… yes, she's fine. But that's not really why I'm here.
questions.poor: Reassurance at this stage can sound dismissive, and it closes the conversation down. An open question keeps it going: ‘How has that been for you and your family?’

questions.q: How old is your dad, and how is his health?
questions.a: He's 60 and he's fine.

questions.q: How old is Lisa?
questions.a: 52, I think.

questions.q: Does your mum have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: Mum is the eldest. Her sister Julie died four years ago, and her brother Mark is 53.

questions.q: What did Julie die of, and how old was she?
questions.a: Ovarian cancer. She was diagnosed at 50 and died at 52.

questions.q: When did your Auntie Julie pass away?
questions.a: Four years ago. It was ovarian cancer.
questions.poor: ‘Pass away’ is gentle, but it can leave the answer vague. For a family history you need the age: ‘How old was Julie when she died?’

questions.q: Does Mark have any children?
questions.a: Mark and his wife Sarah have a daughter, Amy. She's 15.

questions.q: Is Amy their biological daughter, or was she adopted?
questions.a: She was adopted as a baby.
questions.note: Adoption matters for risk: Amy has not inherited anything from this family. Draw her in brackets, with a dashed line to Mark and Sarah.

questions.q: How old is Sarah?
Are your mum's parents still living?
questions.a: Grandad Bill is 84. Grandma Jean died when Mum was a teenager.

questions.q: What did your grandmother Jean die of, and how old was she?
questions.a: She was 47. Mum says it was ‘a women's cancer’. She thinks it was breast cancer, but nobody talked about it then.
questions.note: Record uncertain information as uncertain: ‘d. 47, ?breast cancer’. It may be possible to confirm it later from records.

questions.q: How is your grandfather Bill's health?
questions.a: He had prostate cancer when he was 79. He had treatment and he's doing well.

questions.q: Does your dad have any brothers or sisters?
questions.a: One older brother, Uncle Paul. He's 62 and well.

questions.q: Are your dad's parents still living?
questions.a: Grandma Pat is 82 and well. Grandad Ron died of a heart attack at 70.

questions.q: Has anyone on your dad's side had cancer?
questions.a: Not that I know of.

questions.q: Originally, where did each of your grandparents come from?
questions.a: Mum's parents were both from Swansea. Dad's family are from Manchester, as far back as anyone knows.

questions.q: Is there any Jewish ancestry in the family?
questions.a: No, not that I know of.
questions.note: Some BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants are much more common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, so ask in any family with breast or ovarian cancer.

questions.q: Has anyone in the family had genetic testing?
questions.a: Mum had a test in 2010, after her cancer. She was told nothing was found, but I don't know what they tested.
questions.note: Tests in the past looked at fewer genes, and less thoroughly. An old ‘negative’ result may be worth reviewing.

questions.q: Has anyone else in the family had cancer?
questions.a: Grandad Bill, Julie and Grandma Jean. I think that's everyone.

questions.q: Is there anything you would like to ask me?
questions.a: Just whether I should be having mammograms, and whether my brothers need to worry too.
